transcript:
Meeting Header:
Date: 2026-11-02
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Jasmine Lee (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO, Peregrine), Priya Nair (Head of Platform), Diego Ramirez (Network Engineer)

[00:00:00] Jasmine: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — um, we'll kick off, I'm Jasmine from Redwood AE, and Marcus is our systems engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:06] Liam: Good thanks, bit of a long week but ready to dive in. Thanks for taking time.
[00:00:12] Jasmine: Awesome. Quick agenda: level-set on your network and security reqs, cover Private/VPC options (peering, private endpoints), region constraints, and then outline next steps and pilot. Does that sound right?
[00:00:23] Priya: Yep that's perfect. We're mainly trying to understand what network footprint Redwood needs and how we can maintain strict egress and logging requirements.
[00:00:30] Marcus: Great. I'll start with a quick overview of the Private deployment patterns — there are two common approaches: VPC peering/transit gateway peering to Redwood-managed subnets, or private endpoints (interface endpoints) that hit a customer-managed private link. Both have tradeoffs.
[00:00:45] Diego: Can you clarify what you mean by "Redwood-managed subnets" — do you run instances in our account or in Redwood's account across an interconnect?
[00:00:53] Marcus: Sure. In the Hosted model, Redwood runs everything in our cloud account; Dedicated gives you reserved capacity but still in Redwood infra. For Private, we offer a couple ways: one is Redwood deploys the control plane in our management plane but worker nodes run in a customer VPC (we can run into your account via CloudFormation/ARM templates) or we peer into your VPCs using a transit gateway. Another is private endpoints where traffic stays within your VPC and we expose an interface endpoint that routes to a private load balancer we manage — though that requires cross-account endpoint setup.
[00:01:26] Priya: Ok so if we need everything to stay in our account for compliance, the option is the customer-account worker nodes?
[00:01:33] Marcus: Exactly. We can do an on-prem-style deployment or a customer-account deployment where we provision tenant infra in your cloud account. That gives you full control over egress, routing, and logging.
[00:01:42] Liam: We have a hard requirement that no outbound internet egress is allowed from compute handling customer PII without going through our proxy/inspection stack.
[00:01:50] Marcus: We can support that. In customer-account mode you'd attach NAT/egress controls to the subnets, or you can force all egress through your transit gateway and inspection. We also support static routes so the KV cache and model downloads are pinned, but I should note model updates — if you want automatic model pulls — would need connectivity to our artifact repository unless you host model blobs in an S3 that's accessible in your account.
[00:02:12] Diego: So for model blobs we could mirror them into our S3 and manage access via role assumption?
[00:02:17] Marcus: Yep, that's a pattern we've used. We'll give you a bootstrap script to sync model artifacts into your bucket and the runtime can read from there.
[00:02:24] [00:02:25] Jasmine: Quick question for Diego — do you use a transit gateway currently or multiple VPCs with peering?
[00:02:31] Diego: We use a transit gateway for east-west traffic; we have multiple accounts and use AWS Organizations. We prefer central egress through a set of inspection appliances.
[00:02:40] Marcus: Perfect, transit gateway is a clean integration point — Redwood can peer the worker subnets via TGW attachments or we can deploy agents into your account.
[00:02:49] Priya: Region constraints: we operate in eu-west-1 for the EU datacenter and us-east-1 for US. For EU data residency we need inference to run only in eu-west-1. How flexible is that?
[00:02:59] Marcus: No problem, we can pin model serving to eu-west-1. The dedicated pools and private worker deployment can be region-specific. If you want geo-failover we'll need to plan cross-region replication for KV cache and model artifacts.
[00:03:11] Liam: Latency is a factor — our SLAs for customer-facing features are sub-150ms p99 for short prompts. Does Redwood support local GPUs in eu-west-1 that meet that?
[00:03:19] Marcus: We operate with GPU-backed workers in region; p99 depends on model size and prompt length. For small-medium models we can target that SLA with optimized kernels and batching. For larger models you'd hit longer latencies — we usually suggest a canary to measure.
[00:03:33] [00:03:35] Diego: On KMS/key management — we must bring our own KMS keys for any encryption of model weights or cust data at rest. Is that supported?
[00:03:42] Marcus: Yes, in customer-account deployments you own the KMS keys. Redwood's control plane will store references but never the key material. For Dedicated where resources are Redwood-managed we can integrate with your KMS via cross-account grants or use a customer-managed key in Redwood's account if that's approved.
[00:03:58] Priya: Audit logs and retention: we need audit logs retained for 7 years for certain lines of business; can we push logs to our CloudWatch/Log Storage?
[00:04:06] Marcus: You can forward all runtime logs and traces to an S3/log destination in your account. We also support streaming request/response metadata (redacted) to your SIEM via Kinesis or Fluentd. Full session recordings are heavy — we usually provide a sampling config.
[00:04:20] Jasmine: There's often a question around private endpoints vs peering — in short, peering/TGW gives you more control and less cross-account setup friction if you already manage the TGW; private endpoints can be slightly easier for connectivity but require interface endpoint setup and cross-account permissions.
[00:04:35] Liam: And performance? Which has lower latency?
[00:04:40] Marcus: Peering/TGW is typically lower latency since traffic stays on the backbone; endpoints introduce an extra hop. It's small but measurable at p99.
[00:04:48] Diego: Port requirements — what ports do your workers need open?
[00:04:52] Marcus: Mostly outbound HTTPS (443) for artifact pulls unless you mirror artifacts. For intra-cluster we use gRPC over defined ports; we'll provide a list.
[00:04:59] Priya: For compliance we need SAML SSO, SCIM provisioning, role-based access controls, and enterprise audit evidence. Do you support SCIM?
[00:05:08] Jasmine: Yes SAML + SCIM supported, RBAC with role mapping, and we can provide SOC2 Type II reports and customer-specific audit packs under NDA.
[00:05:16] [00:05:18] Liam: Ok, switching to pricing — high level, what does a 6-week pilot with private deployment cost? We're trying to budget.
[00:05:24] Jasmine: I'll send a tailored pricing sheet, but ballpark the pilot includes an onboarding fee for the Private setup, reserved GPU hours for the pilot, and a support engagement. We'll send numbers after this call.
[00:05:33] Marcus: From a technical side, for the pilot we recommend a small worker pool pinned in eu-west-1 with constraints so we can measure latency and cost. We'll need a test dataset and sample prompts to run benchmarks.
[00:05:44] Priya: For the benchmarks — we want both latency and cost per 1k tokens measured with our prompt patterns.
[00:05:50] Marcus: Yep, we'll run the eval harness and share token-level cost breakdown.
[00:05:55] Jasmine: Diego, could you share your VPC CIDR ranges and the TGW attachment account ids? That will help Marcus prepare the network plan.
[00:06:03] Diego: Sure, I can pull that post-call. We'll need to validate any ACLs on the TGW side too.
[00:06:08] [00:06:15] Liam: About fallbacks — suppose capacity in eu-west-1 is constrained, can we failover to us-east-1 but keep data residency?
[00:06:22] Marcus: If data residency is strict, automatic cross-region failover would violate that. We can set policy-based routing so requests from EU customers only hit EU workers; fallback to another region would require legal/ops approvals and maybe anonymization. We often set up routing policies to prevent accidental cross-region failover.
[00:06:41] Priya: Also curious about private endpoints for vendor management — some of our security folks want the vendor to not run anything in our account but allow private endpoint access. Is that acceptable?
[00:06:50] Marcus: It's acceptable, but then you trade off control: we manage infra but you get a private interface. You still need to agree on egress patterns and logs; some customers pair this with a flow log mirror.
[00:06:59] Diego: For cross-account endpoint, what's the auth model? VPC endpoint policies + IAM?
[00:07:04] Marcus: Right, we use endpoint policies and cross-account IAM roles to enforce access. We'll provide sample CloudFormation to standardize the setup.
[00:07:12] [00:07:18] Jasmine: There were a couple of product nitty-gritty things Marcus — can you run through KV caching and how that behaves in the private setup?
[00:07:24] Marcus: Sure — Redis-style KV caching sits alongside the runtime. In customer-account deployments you can provision the cache in your VPC; the runtime will hit local cache, which reduces model context rebuilds. Note: sometimes transcripts auto-gen writes KV cache as "KV cash" — small typos.
[00:07:39] [00:07:42] Priya: Haha noted. On logging again, do you support audit log immutability or WORM retention?
[00:07:48] Marcus: For logs you can push to S3 with Object Lock for WORM. If you want tamper-evident logs we recommend that.
[00:07:55] Liam: Any certifications we should care about? SOC2 Type II is critical; ISO is nice to have.
[00:08:01] Jasmine: We have SOC2 Type II and are working toward ISO 27001; I'll include the control mapping doc.
[00:08:07] [00:08:12] Diego: One more technical question — do you support VPC peering with overlapping CIDRs? We do have some legacy ranges that overlap with partners.
[00:08:19] Marcus: Overlapping CIDRs complicate peering; you can use NAT translations at the TGW or use PrivateLink which avoids overlap issues. We'll advise on the best pattern once we see your ranges.
[00:08:31] Priya: In terms of operational ownership, who handles patching of the runtime when it's in our account?
[00:08:36] Marcus: If we deploy workers into your account, patching can be run by Redwood via delegated role or you can run it yourself; we provide the release artifacts and a patch orchestration playbook. For Dedicated in Redwood accounts we handle patching on our maintenance windows.
[00:08:50] [00:08:55] Jasmine: Okay let's talk deliverables — we'll send: security pack and SOC2, a sample CloudFormation/terraform for VPC/TGW attachments, pricing sheet for pilot, and a proposed schedule for the network deep-dive.
[00:09:07] Liam: Sounds good. Anything else from our side?
[00:09:10] Priya: We'll prepare a short list of pilot success criteria (latency, throughput, cost per 1k tokens) and share before the design call.
[00:09:16] Jasmine: Perfect.
[00:09:18] [00:09:25] --- (discussion continues with clarifying questions, slight crosstalk, and scheduling) ---
[00:30:00] Marcus: (mid-call) we also support hardware pinning — if you need deterministic performance we can pin to a dedicated GPU family in-region.
[00:30:10] Diego: That would be useful for benchmarks — we can provide sample prompt mix.
[00:30:17] Marcus: Great.
[00:42:00] Liam: Quick final question about network egress IPs — do you publish static egress IPs for the service?
[00:42:07] Marcus: For Hosted we publish ranges; for Private customer-account deployments you control egress IPs. If we manage egress from Redwood side we can allocate static elastic IPs and publish them behind a managed NAT.
[00:42:20] Priya: Ok that resolves the firewall rule concerns.
[00:42:25] Jasmine: Alright, recap of next steps: Jasmine to send security and pricing, Marcus to schedule the network deep-dive and prepare infra templates, Diego to share CIDR/TGW info, and Peregrine to draft pilot success criteria. We aim to have the network deep-dive week of Nov 9.
[00:42:40] Liam: Thanks everyone — we'll review the pack and get Diego's info by Friday.
[00:42:46] Jasmine: Thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.
Notes: small transcription errors present (product names occasionally mis-typed), references to artifacts: security whitepaper (link: https://redwood.example/sec-whitepaper), sample infra repo (link: https://github.com/redwood-inference/private-deploy-samples).
